metadata.description: Declassified in Part - Sanitized Copy Approved for Release 2016/07/05 : CIA-RDP79T00024A000200010013-1 The President's Daily Brief August 16, 1976 2 Top Secret Declassified in Part - Sanitized Copy Approved for Release 2016/07/05 : CIA-RDP79T00024A000200010013-1 Declassified in Part - Sanitized Copy Approved for Release 2016/07/05 : CIA-RDP79T00024A000200010013-1 Exempt from general declassification schedule of EQ 11652 exemption category 5B( declassified only on approval of the Director of Central Intelligence Declassified in Part - Sanitized Copy Approved for Release 2016/07/05 : CIA-RDP79T00024A000200010013-1 Declassified in Part - Sanitized Copy Approved for Release 2016/07/05 : CIA-RDP79T00024A000200010013-1 FOR THE PRESIDENT ONLY August 16, 1976 Table of Contents Lebanon: The Christians have launched efforts to retake Pales-tinian positions in the mountains east of Beirut and to tighten the siege of Tripoli. The newly arrived Iraqi con-tingent is moving to consolidate control of the Sidon-Beirut highway. (Page 1) Egypt-Syria: An exchange of denunciations over the weekend has opened a new chapter in Egyptian-Syrian political warfare. (Page 3) Egypt-Libya: Egyptian officials assume Libya was behind the bombing of a passenger train in Alexandria on Saturday. It warned "all these traitors who call themselves Arabs that the battle to purge them from honorable Arab ranks has begun." Although Egypt's statement seemed to give official sanction to re-cent hints in the Cairo press that the Syrian regime should be top-pled, there is little that the Egyptians can do directly to bring the Asad government down. They could, however, step up their al-ready considerable effort to rearm Palestinian and leftist forces in Lebanon. Syria responded on Saturday with an equally scornful but less threat-ening official statement that re-hashed old Syrian charges of Egyp-tian cooperation with Israel and for the first time publicly accused Egypt of supplying arms to Pales-tinian forces in Lebanon. This pos-sibility reportedly was considered and rejected last month. The Egyptians are already assisting in the transport of Iraqi militia-men to Lebanon. metadata.description: Hamdane Ben Othman Khodja (1773- entre 1840 et 1845) était un notable et un savant d'Alger . Il a écrit Le Miroir dans lequel il dénonce les exactions des soldats français à Alger peu après la conquête de l'Algérie par la France. Hamdane Ben Othman Khodja appartient à une famille de notables algérois, son père, Othman, un jurisconsulte de renom, jouissait d’une grande estime auprès de l’administration de la Régence d'Alger, représentée à sa plus haute échelle par le dey. Ayant montré des compétences inouïes en matière de lois, le dey lui confia la supervision des comptes budgétaires et les dossiers contenant les noms et les grades, ainsi que les traitements des janissaires. En plus de l’administration, le père de Hamdane exerçait également le métier d’enseignant qu’il transmettra plus tard à son fils. Son oncle Mohammed Hadj, quant à lui, s’occupait de Dar El Seka, l’équivalent de l’Hôtel des Monnaies de nos jours.   Khodja est né à Alger en 1773 dans une famille d'origine turque appartenant à la haute administration de la régence d'Alger . Son père était un lettré koloughli, un ouléma et le defterdar de la Régence, et sa mère, une mauresque. Il reçut une excellente éducation et voyagea beaucoup . En 1784, lorsque son oncle eut la responsabilité de porter un cadeau du dey à Istanbul, il l'accompagna. Après son retour d’Istanbul, Hamdane passa à une étape supérieure de son apprentissage, il se consacra ainsi à l’étude de la philosophie, de la théologie et des sciences de son temps. La médecine occupait une partie importante de cette passion dévouée au savoir. Il écrira plus tard un ouvrage traitant des moyens de se prémunir de l’épidémie et qu’il intitula Ithaf al mounsifin wa el odaba fi el ihtiraz min el ouaba (Le don fait aux justes et aux lettrés pour se prémunir des maladies épidémiques). Après la mort de son père, il lui succéda comme enseignant en théologie puis rapidement son oncle le prit dans son affaire et l'envoya le représenter dans des villes comme Tunis, Livourne, Marseille, Londres et Gibraltar, lui donnant ainsi l'occasion d'apprendre le turc, le français et l'anglais . Khodja devint un des marchands les plus importants et les plus riches d'Alger, où il était très sollicité par des collègues désireux d'être associés à ses opérations commerciales qui s'étendaient à l'empire ottoman comme à l'Europe .     Après l’occupation d’Alger, il fut nommé membre de la municipalité que Bourmont constitua. Selon H. Khodja, ce n’était qu’une mascarade, car : « Les délibérations étaient silencieuses et pour la forme ; enfin notre participation était nulle au fond ». En sa qualité de membre du conseil municipal d'Alger ,il participa à la commission française d'indemnisation des personnes dont les biens avaient été démolis pour cause "d'utilité publique" jusqu'à la dissolution de cette commission et la fin des indemnisations. Il servit ensuite d'intermédiaire entre le bey de Constantine, Hadj Ahmed et les Français   Face aux exactions commises par les troupes françaises, il rédigea en 1833 un manuscrit qui se voulait à la fois historique et politique, Aperçu historique et statistique sur la régence d’Alger, intitulé en arabe al Mir’āt’ (Le Miroir). Un témoignage qui demeure avant tout, un plaidoyer et un réquisitoire : un plaidoyer en faveur de la Régence et un réquisitoire contre l’administration de Bourmont et de Clauzel. Le manuscrit a été écrit par lui en arabe, et a été traduit en français par H.-D. Oriental et publié à Paris en 1833 aux éditons Goetchy fils et Cie; sous le titre [Aperçu historique et statistique sur la régence d'Alger, intitulé en arabe : "Le Miroir" ; par sidy Hamdan-Ben-Othman-Khoja,... Traduit de l'arabe par H.... D..  1833.  ]   Une "Réfutation de l'ouvrage de Sidi Hamdan" parut dans l'Observateur des Tribunaux en 1834 à quoi Hamdan Khodja répliqua, la même année et dans la même revue, par une "Réponse au maréchal Clauzel", ce dernier étant vraisemblablement l'auteur de la "réfutation" Les initiales H.-D. poussent à croire que le travail de traduction fut l’œuvre du Tripolitain (Tripoli d’al Gharb)  : Hassouna Daghiss (Hassuna D’ghies.). Pourtant, Personne ne peut affirmer ni infirmer, si c’est bien lui l’auteur de la traduction, car H. Khodja, lui-même, ne le confirme pas. Ce dernier, dans une lettre datée du 28 décembre 1833 qu’il adresse au général Voirol, écrivit que l’ouvrage a été imprimé à Paris et, que son fils Hassan en aurait reçu un exemplaire qu’il devait remettre à la Commission [ Commission d’Afrique, créée pour enquêter sur la situation en Algérie ] . Chose qui n’a pas pu se faire car le livre arriva tardivement. Par contre, il ordonna à son fils de le remettre au général afin qu’il examine son travail : « J’ai donné ordre à mon fils de vous le remettre et je réclame .de votre justice d’examiner ce travail sans faire attention à son auteur, car chacun écrit d’après l’éducation qu’il a reçu et de son propre jugement ». D’ailleurs, ce qui est singulier c’est que dans le Miroir, il ne fait aucune allusion à l’aide que lui aurait apportée Daghiss : en effet, la seule fois où il parle de lui, c’est quand il souligne la traduction que fit ce dernier de l’œuvre de Vattel, traduction qu’il a fait du français vers l’arabe. le mémoire a été publié en annexe du livre de Michel Habart intitulé  "Histoire d'un parjure". La question est : pourquoi ne l’a-t-il pas clairement spécifié, étant donné qu’il ne manque pas de le féliciter pour son travail de traducteur : « Je ne lis pas le français, cependant j’ai bien connaissance de la traduction fidèle en arabe, que M. le chérif Hassuna Deguiz a faite du droit des gens de Wattel ». Le texte original en arabe du Miroir n’a jamais été retrouvé, seule la version en français existe ; et c’est à partir de cette dernière, qu’il fut traduit, présenté et commenté en langue arabe par Mohamed Larbi Z’biri. [ ( 1985), Al Mir‛āt  Alger, SNED. ] Sans mettre en doute l’authenticité ou réfuter l’ouvrage ,l’original aurait mieux permis d’appréhender toute la richesse du texte et d’en exploiter les idées et, surtout de mettre fin aux doutes et aux rumeurs qui supposaient que le manuscrit avait été écrit par un publiciste français, donc n’aurait jamais été traduit. D’autre part, il existe une autre publication du Miroir où le texte est suivi d’une réfutation des amis du maréchal Clauzel ainsi que d’une réponse à la réfutation En 2009, lors du symposium organisé à Alger, portant sur thème « L’Algérie, durant la période ottomane : Les relations politiques, économiques et culturelles », les Archives Nationales d’Alger (A.N.A) se sont vues offrir par le gouvernement turc, deux manuscrits écrits en langue arabe. Le premier, intitulé  "Le Miroir d'Alger" (" مرآة الجزائر "), écrit en 1837 par Mohamed Redha, le fils de H. Khodja et le second est une copie d’un deuxième livre de H. Khodja dans lequel il traite et appuie les réformes engagées par le sultan ottoman, Abdelhamid II » Le Miroir se divise en deux parties. La première est répartie en douze chapitres, les six premiers sont consacrés à décrire le pays, les habitants en faisant d’eux des êtres attachants, respectueux de leurs traditions ancestrales. Nous remarquons que pour désigner les habitants : Algérois, Kabyles, Arabes, Turcs ou Kouloughlis, il utilise le mot « Algériens », est-ce à dire que déjà les notions d’État et de nation avaient pris forme dans son esprit, et que de ce fait, il pouvait les appliquer à la Régence en rassemblant les différentes communautés qui se côtoyaient sans vraiment avoir à l’esprit ce sentiment d’unité ? Était-il le seul à le penser ou bien d’autres partageaient-ils sa vision ? Car par rapport aux correspondances qu’il adressait à l’administration turque, et telles qu’elles ont été traduites en arabe, nous pouvons observer que les vocables utilisées généralement pour désigner les populations sont « ‛ahl » ou « raʽiyya » ou sujets ou tout simplement il oppose les musulmans aux infidèles. Les chapitres restants sont consacrés au gouvernement, à ses lois et à sa législation. Il insiste sur le fait que la Régence était un État fondé sur des principes républicains, qui n’a rien à voir avec un État corsaire sans foi ni loi comme le pensait l’Europe, Il écrit :   « Dans le cours de mon voyage en Europe, j’ai étudié les principes de la liberté européenne qui fait la base d’un gouvernement représentatif et républicain. J’ai trouvé que ces principes étaient semblables aux principes fondamentaux de notre législation, si ce n’est qu’il existe une différence imperceptible dans l’application ». Toutefois, il ne nie pas l’aspect négatif de certains deys, de leurs erreurs qui ont entrainé le déclin de l’État algérien et l’occupation française. La seconde partie relate le début de l’occupation française, de son administration et des erreurs tactiques et des exactions commises envers la population et ses biens. Il met l’accent sur les promesses non tenues de certains généraux, il les accuse d’avoir déshonoré leur intégrité ; c’est la partie miroir ou la partie négative de l’occupation, son but étant de faire passer un message libéral et de toucher l’opinion publique sur la question de l’indépendance de l’Algérie. Ce n’est plus le Turc ni le Kouloughli qui parle mais l’Algérien qui est attaché à sa patrie : » […] chez nous nous n’étions pas hommes d’ Etat , ce n’est que sur cette terre que nous avons acquis nos titres, et nos dignités… ; ce pays est donc notre patrie !  ». Avant de poursuivre, cette citation mérite que l’on s’y arrête, car elle soulève plusieurs interrogations par rapport à la perception de « patrie » qui elle-même renvoie à des interrogations sur les notions de peuple, de communauté et de nation. Ainsi, lorsque H. Khodja   parle de patrie il désignait sa terre natale, et par peuple(s) l’ensemble des communautés de la Régence qui formaient une nation, un peuple de tribus tous unis par leur attachement à leur terre. Après avoir en vain demandé au Sultan ottoman d'intervenir, il quitta Paris en 1836 pour s'établir à Istanbul où il mourut entre 1840 et 1845.

metadata.description: Abstract: The article offers a concise topographical and archaeological examination of the sites between Derna and Cyrene that Claude Le Maire, French consul in Tripoli de Barbarie, mentions in a record about his travels in Cyrenaica (1705-6), reading the accounts of nineteenth-century travelers (esp. J.R. Pacho) and using recent studies, cartographic data from 1931-6 and updated satellite data. The article explores Le Maire's units of measurement for distances (“lieues” and “heures de chemin”). It also focuses on two sites of uncertain name and location (Lais and Turte – or Tuste or Juste). Finally, the article analyzes different potential routes through this area of Cyrenaica and the possibility that Le Maire's observations are related to different trips following partially diverse itineraries. L’articolo propone una sintetica revisione topografica ed archeologica dei siti che Claude Le Maire, console francese a Tripoli de Barbarie, menziona tra Derna e Cirene nella memoria originale del viaggio effettuato in Cirenaica (1705-6), rileggendo i resoconti dei viaggiatori del XIX (in part. J.R. Pacho) e gli studi recenti, utilizzando altresì dati cartografici del 1931-6 e satellitari aggiornati. Si affrontano le modalità di indicazione delle distanze usate da Le Maire (lieues e heures de chemin) e ci si sofferma in part. sui due siti di incerta denominazione ed ubicazione (Lais, e Turte – o Tuste o Juste). Si analizzano in conclusione i diversi percorsi possibili di questo settore della Cirenaica, e la possibilità che le osservazioni di Le Maire siano relative diversi viaggi, in parte effettuati lungo itinerari diversi.

metadata.creator: Trémaux, P. (Pierre) photographer
description: Pierre Trémaux (1818-1895) was a French architect, photographer, traveler and writer of scientific and ethnographic texts. Beginning in 1847 he recorded his expeditions to Asia Minor, Egypt, Libya and Tunisia first in sketches and daguerreotypes and then in calotypes for greater veracity, all of which were also reproduced as lithographs in his publications

The volume depicting the landscapes, architecture and people of North Africa, contains 57 plates of illustrations (49 lithographs and eight calotypes) and four maps made during Trémaux's second expedition
Issued in parts
To accompany the author's Voyage en Éthiopie, au Soudan oriental et dans la Nigritie. Paris : L. Hachette, 1862-[1863]
Title from title page
Title on spine: P. Trémaux / Voyages au Soundan oriental
Plates 36, 38, 44, 46, 47, 50, 52 and 55 are calotypes and depict both portraits and landscapes
The illustrations are numbered 1 through 56; number 55 is present both as a calotype and as a lithograph. A man leading a donkey laden with firewood has been added to the foreground of the lithograph
Lithographers include: Laurens; Tirpenne; Didiere; V. Adam; A. Adam; Pinque; Decon; Gaildrau and E. David
Printers of plates include Godard and Lemercier
Half calf binding with gilt tooled spine and marbled paper covers

metadata.creator: Profiles in History
metadata.description: Profiles in History: Autograph Auction 34 Winter 2002 Auction Highlights include: Erwin Rommel's raw, triumphant postcard sent on the literal opening week of WWII. Harry Truman's unedited reflections on brawling with Stalin and Churchill at Potsdam. Daniel Boone's hand-drawn Kentucky boundary logs. FDR's localized 1927 ballot where he hand-wrote Eleanor Roosevelt into local office. Presidential & Foundational Era John Adams (December 10, 1799): An exceptionally rare official letter signed as President to the U.S. Senate. Adams explicitly praises the promptitude and zeal of federal troops used to crush the Fries Rebellion in eastern Pennsylvania. The catalog highlights a fascinating backstory: local farmers revolted over direct property taxes passed to fund defense against France. While Adams declared the riot a "highhanded" dangerous affair, he determined it wasn't treason and eventually issued a full pardon—a move that cost him critical support from his own conservative Federalist Party during the tight election of 1800. John Quincy Adams (June 6, 1791): A rare early autograph letter signed to a legal colleague named "Putnam". Written right after his admission to the bar, Adams coordinates a legal writ before playfully adding that the intricate question posed to him is too perplexing for a busy day, proposing they instead discuss it soon over "a segar [cigar] & glass of wine". John Quincy Adams Stock Certificate (April 17, 1809): An original stock certificate for the Boylston Market Association, signed by Adams as its very first president. The historic market complex was built far out of town at the time and named after Adams' second cousin, Ward Nicholas Boylston. James Bowdoin (March 30, 1786): An important Revolutionary War-era letter signed as Governor of Massachusetts to the Governor of North Carolina. Bowdoin officially states that Massachusetts has acceded to Virginia's proposal to hold the Annapolis Convention in Maryland to regulate interstate trade. This meeting ultimately served as the critical precursor to the 1787 Philadelphia Convention, where the weak Articles of Confederation were discarded in favor of the U.S. Constitution. James Buchanan (March 13, 1859): An exceptional pre-Civil War letter signed as President to Indian Affairs Commissioner James Denver. Buchanan voices deep gratitude for Denver's firm, impartial leadership as the territorial Governor of Kansas during the incredibly violent "Bleeding Kansas" border wars. Millard Fillmore (September 15, 1869): A handwritten letter showing a warm kinship between two U.S. presidents. Fillmore writes to voice his deep relief that the newly inaugurated Chief Executive, Ulysses S. Grant, had returned home safely and was on the path to recovering his health after an unexpected illness forced him to miss the New York State Fair. James A. Garfield (April 15, 1881): An exceptionally rare official letter of state signed as President. Garfield authorizes the Secretary of State to affix the Seal of the United States to his formal reply to a congratulatory message from the Republic of San Marino. Because Garfield was tragically shot by an assassin just two and a half months later, documents signed during his brief 6-month presidency are of immense rarity. James A. Garfield on Lincoln's Funeral (May 2, 1865): A poignant handwritten letter written as a Representative from Ohio to Speaker of the House Schuyler Colfax. Garfield writes from his home state to describe traveling to Cleveland to meet Abraham Lincoln’s slow-moving funeral train. He expresses deep regret that Colfax was unable to accompany the cortege, creating an incredible historical link between the first and second U.S. presidents to be assassinated. Andrew Jackson Walking Cane Letter (c. January/February 1831): An exceptional letter signed as President to a Virginia resident, typed out by his adopted son. Jackson warmly accepts a presentation walking cane carved from a tree that stood on the physical battlefield of the Battle of New Orleans. Jackson praises the brave men whose valor served as the "Security of the Union," referencing the legendary War of 1812 victory that vaulted his military persona into the White House. Andrew Jackson Land Grant (January 1, 1830): A document signed as President on vellum, granting a 113-acre plot of land located near St. Louis, Missouri. Thomas Jefferson & the UVA Rotunda (October 7, 1823): A magnificent autograph letter signed from Monticello to Master Carpenter James Oldham. Writing as the "Father of the University of Virginia," the aging former president outlines the ongoing construction of the university's famous architectural crown jewel, the UVA Rotunda. Jefferson rejects Oldham’s direct financial appeals to the Board of Visitors regarding a wage dispute, telling him that contractual adjustments must go through the executive proctor or the ordinary courts. This exact letter famously triggered the very first lawsuit brought against the University of Virginia. Thomas Jefferson Navy Commission (March 16, 1807): An exceptional document signed as President (countersigned by Navy Secretary Robert Smith) commissioning Hethcote J. Reed as a Lieutenant. Reed served as a midshipman on the historic frigate USS Constitution ("Old Ironsides") during the Barbary Coast patrols and fought in the celebrated assault on Tripoli during the Tripolitan War. Thomas Jefferson & James Madison Ships' Papers (December 30, 1806): A large folio-sized safe-passage document signed jointly by Jefferson as President and Madison as Secretary of State. The document features a rare four-language parallel text configuration (English, Dutch, French, and Spanish) granting passage to a brig carrying livestock and lumber out of an American port. William Henry Harrison Political Overtures (July 12, 1837): A dense, 4-page political strategy letter written to Whig organizer Silas M. Stilwell. Harrison plots with party allies Daniel Webster and Henry Clay to overthrow the Jacksonian Democrats in the upcoming 1840 election. Harrison warns his party to respect their opponents' perfect discipline, delivering a timeless political axiom: "Confidence in the weakness of our enemy has produced the most disastrous defeats on record." John F. Kennedy Handwritten Note (January 10, 1962): An incredibly rare autograph letter signed as President on official green White House stationery. Writing to a former Senate colleague ("Senator Martin"), Kennedy sends friendly New Year's greetings, marking one of only a handful of full one-page handwritten presidential letters from JFK in private hands. Herbert Hoover Signed Portrait (Undated): A handsome sepia portrait photograph of the smartly dressed president, warmly inscribed to a local doctor. Herbert Hoover anti-FDR Rant (September 3, 1934): A scathing 2-page typed letter attacking the newly formed "American Liberty League". Hoover accuses the disgruntled corporate Democrats backing the league of hijacking the 1932 Republican platform, bluntly declaring that he has no more confidence in their Wall Street model of liberty than the New Deal model. Herbert Hoover Teapot Dome Speech (November 14, 1933): A signed 5-page transcript of the speech Hoover delivered at the dedication of the Warren G. Harding Memorial. Hoover fiercely castigates the corrupt Teapot Dome conspirators for violating public trust. Historically, Teapot Dome ringleader Harry M. Daugherty sat seething barely thirty feet away in the audience as Hoover spoke. James Madison War-Date Letter (January 5, 1813): A superb presidential letter written marked "private" to his newly elected Vice President, Elbridge Gerry. Madison answers technical questions regarding taking the constitutional oath of office. He urges the aging Gerry to travel south to Virginia to avoid the harsh winter weather, writing: "Your friends in Virginia will then be the gainers..." The catalog highlights that Gerry followed Madison's advice and took his oath at home in Cambridge before taking his seat as president pro tempore of the Senate. This letter is also famous for detailing the origin of the term "gerrymander," coined after Gerry distorted Massachusetts voting districts to look like a salamander. James Madison Cabinet Strife Letter (August 29, 1810): A fascinating autograph letter signed as President to his bitter political rival, Senator Samuel Smith. Madison handles tense complaints regarding Treasury deposits and defends his embattled Treasury Secretary, Albert Gallatin. This letter captures a highly unstable moment in Madison's administration, balancing a divided cabinet alongside a deteriorating relationship with Napoleon on the brink of the War of 1812. James Madison Ship's Passport (June 1, 1811): A scallop-top ship's passport signed on vellum by President Madison, countersigned by Secretary of State Robert Smith, granting safe passage to a two-gun schooner named the Fly of Bristol. James K. Polk Grandfather Vindication (August 24, 1844): A handwritten campaign letter marked "Private" to a Nashville editor. Polk fiercely defends against toxic Whig character attacks that accused his grandfather, Col. Ezekiel Polk, of being a Revolutionary War Tory (a British loyalist). Polk biography notes that Polk became entirely obsessed with this issue, spending more energy defending his grandfather's memory than almost any other topic in the tight 1844 election. Franklin D. Roosevelt Scripture Beliefs (January 6, 1929): A typed letter written as Governor of New York to a Texas reverend, explicitly confirming his deep reliance on the Bible: "Please understand that I read the Scriptures and believe in the Book from cover to cover, and am trying to carry out the teaching of the Master as best I can." Franklin D. Roosevelt Disabled Veterans Message (December 24, 1935): A moving typed letter signed as President, delivered on Christmas Eve to a World War I veterans organization. Roosevelt praises the noble living and noble dead, offering the everlasting gratitude of the nation they served. Franklin D. Roosevelt Dutchess County Absentee Ballot (November 8, 1927): An extraordinary legal voting archive completed and signed three times by FDR just before his election as Governor of New York. Voting an all-Democrat ticket, Roosevelt casts a vote against the extension of the New York Governor's term (a historic irony given he would later break all boundaries by winning four terms as President). Best of all, on the local town section, Roosevelt explicitly hand-writes in his wife, Eleanor Roosevelt, as School Director for Hyde Park. Eleanor Roosevelt on Joseph P. Kennedy (June 21): A rare handwritten letter signed as First Lady to her son James. Eleanor recounts hosting a porch picnic lunch for the Kennedy family patriarch, Joseph P. Kennedy, leaving a sharp and incredibly shrewd historical assessment of the future ambassador: "Joe Kennedy has been here... I enjoyed listening to him. A complete egotist but an intelligent & kindly one." Harry S. Truman on Potsdam & McCarthy (May 28, 1954): A spectacular 6-page autograph letter signed "Harry" to his former Secretary of State, Dean Acheson. Truman recounts working on his memoirs 17 hours a day and relives an exasperated clash he had at the Potsdam Conference with Winston Churchill and Joseph Stalin regarding Spanish dictator Francisco Franco. He tells Acheson that he snapped at the dictators, declaring he didn't come to Berlin to run a "police court". When translated, Stalin roared with laughter and suggested they talk about Poland instead. Truman then transitions to domestic affairs, bluntly observing that the ongoing Sen. Joseph McCarthy anti-communist hearings are causing massive shame to his Republican friends. He sharply criticizes the Eisenhower White House as "smart but inexperienced boys" who are upsetting NATO and throwing away America's military strength while dangerously eyeing intervention in Indo-China. Harry S. Truman on JFK & the 1960 Convention (July 9, 1960): Another remarkable handwritten letter signed "Harry" to Dean Acheson, penned just two days before the 1960 Democratic National Convention. Truman writes that party leaders are begging him to attend, adding that he intends to "have a lot of fun with the guessers and the prophets." The catalog notes that Truman strongly disliked John F. Kennedy, previously calling him too inexperienced and publicly demanding: "Senator, are you certain that you are quite ready for the country?" Woodrow Wilson on the British Blockade (March 19, 1915): A typed letter signed as President, accompanied by a hand-corrected 4-page Letter of State addressed to Great Britain regarding their aggressive naval blockade off Germany. Wilson warns the British government that their unusually massive shipping cordon violates international law by burdening neutral American merchantmen. This warning was terrifyingly on-point: just two weeks later, the German navy retaliated against the blockade zone, sinking the passenger liner Lusitania and drowning nearly 200 Americans. Woodrow Wilson Literature Quote (October 16, 1899): A beautiful, signed autograph quote penned while serving as the President of Princeton University: "Literature is a thing of convictions, of insights, of what is felt and seen and heard and hoped for."Zachary Taylor (June 19, 1850): An incredibly rare letter signed as President, written to New York Governor Hamilton Fish less than one month before Taylor's sudden death in office. Taylor declines an invitation to the New York State Fair, noting that he cannot leave Washington while Congress is aggressively debating the highly controversial Compromise of 1850 regarding the extension of slavery. Taylor fell ill five days after July 4th and passed away from rampaging cholera. William H. Taft on the League of Nations (December 18, 1920): A typed letter signed regarding a controversy over the omission of any reference to God in the preamble to the League of Nations' charter. Taft notes he would have strongly favored a recognition of the Deity, but argues that the omission wasn't sinister and doesn't justify a big debate, concluding: "Preambles are not the substance of the League, and it is about the substance that we are interested." Civil War, Military, & Global Affairs Jefferson Davis (March 20, 1863): A high-stakes Civil War-date letter signed as President of the C.S.A. to Georgia Governor J.E. Brown. Davis addresses a tense military incident where Confederate General Braxton Bragg ordered his quartermasters to use armed force, if necessary, to seize control of Georgia's state-owned Western & Atlantic Railroad after transit workers allegedly refused to transport Southern munitions. Davis acts as an urgent diplomat, regretting the general's extra-legal threats and smoothing over state-versus-federal tensions with a plea for Southern solidarity. Turner Ashby (February 29, 1862): A highly scarce Confederate army receipt signed by Ashby as Colonel in Winchester, Virginia, securing transport wagons and horses. Ashby was one of "Stonewall" Jackson's most trusted cavalry subordinates and was tragically killed in action just three months later. Ellis Spear of the 20th Maine (Undated): A fascinating 5-page original autograph manuscript recounting the close-quarters horrors of the 1864 Wilderness Campaign and the Battle of Spotsylvania Court House. Spear, who took command of the legendary regiment after Joshua Chamberlain was promoted, reflects on the exhausting night marches and constant skirmishes that were enough to make a veteran tired just thinking about it decades later. Joshua L. Chamberlain & Thomas D. Chamberlain (October 12, 1870): A unique historical check filled out by the "Savior of Gettysburg" and signed jointly by both famous brothers. Thomas served as a captain under Joshua, and famously survived a near-fatal close-range gun encounter while successfully securing the Union's left flank on Little Round Top. William F. Smith (March 11, 1891): A candid post-war letter where the former Union Major General admits he is writing a defense paper to evaluate the battlefield performance of General Grant. Smith controversially concludes that General Grant was a poor military commander compared to Confederate generals, echoing a highly unpopular public opinion at the time. Edward Townsend (March 30, 1865): An official State Department invitation presented to the Governor of Missouri to witness the historic flag-raising ceremony at Fort Sumter. Scheduled for April 14, 1865—exactly four years to the day after the fort fell—the event allowed General Robert Anderson to re-raise the very same tattered garrison flag that had marked the literal start of the Civil War. David Ben-Gurion (March 13, 1954): A powerful letter handwritten in Hebrew from his retreat in Sde Boker to a Knesset member. Ben-Gurion issues a stark warning to "naive" pacifists, declaring that Israel must rid itself of illusions that external Jewish organizations can guarantee safety from border raids, fiercely arguing that the sole security of Israel lies with the IDF. Catherine the Great (January 9, 1793): A beautiful, tender New Year's greeting letter written in French by the Russian Empress to her sister, the Princess of Anhalt-Zerbst. Abraham Lincoln Legal Opinion (August 17, 1850): A full-page autograph letter signed from Springfield, Illinois, regarding a civil land title dispute. Evaluating a forged property deed, Lincoln delivers a characteristically blunt and succinct legal assessment: "This is the whole story — The case can not be gained by much talking." Abraham Lincoln Circuit Court Receipt (May 1, 1858): A handwritten financial document signed as an Illinois general practice attorney. Dated just six weeks before his famous "House Divided" speech propelled him to national visibility, Lincoln signs off on court fees received for a case in the Vermilion Circuit Court. Robert E. Lee Lexington Correspondence (June 22, 1866): A gracious 2-page letter written as President of Washington College to a former Union soldier, Major Richard P. Hammond. Writing just one year after the war ended, Lee attempts to track down a missing Confederate general on behalf of his former battlefield adversary, showcasing the smooth, respectful resumption of peace between North and South. Robert E. Lee Signature (March 8, 1869): A bold, clean ink signature reading "R.E. Lee," clipped from a larger document. John Hancock Military Appointment (July 1, 1775): A spectacular Revolutionary War document signed boldly by Hancock as President of the Continental Congress, countersigned by Charles Thomson. Hancock appoints an ensign to the Massachusetts Regiment just two weeks after the bloody Battle of Bunker Hill, and a mere two days before George Washington arrived in Cambridge to assume formal command of the Continental Army. Julia Ward Howe Battle Hymn of the Republic Manuscript (March 21, 1865): A monumental piece of American cultural history. A complete 2-page autograph manuscript of her famous Union rallying anthem, written entirely in her hand and signed just two weeks before Robert E. Lee's surrender at Appomattox. Incredibly, this specific copy features an un-published extra stanza attacking god's contemners that did not make it into the final Atlantic Monthly printing. Francis Gary Powers U-2 Spy Flight Letter (September 22, 1970): A rare typed letter signed by the famous Cold War pilot to an aviation magazine editor. Powers reviews a book tracking the history of aerial reconnaissance, commenting on the super-secret CIA U-2 program that caused an international crisis when he was shot down over downtown Moscow in 1960. Theodor Herzl Zionist Letter (August 10, 1902): A printed political letter signed by the zionist leader from Vienna. Written right as critical negotiations with the Ottoman Empire collapsed, Herzl outlines the upcoming agenda for the Zionist Action Committee, which marked his historic shift to lobby the British government for a Jewish homeland. Nathaniel Lyon Pre-Battle Report (May 12, 1861): An exceptionally rare Civil War letter written from the St. Louis Arsenal just three months before Lyon was killed in action. Writing to the Adjutant General, Lyon reports on a local clash where Union troops and a civilian mob engaged in a deadly shootout, killing 12 people. Lyon openly criticizes his brash superior, General William S. Harney, warning that Harney's erratic city orders painfully embarrass his covert strategy to stop pro-Confederate combinations from seizing the state of Missouri. Philip H. Sheridan Legendary War Horse Letter (March 24, 1876): A wonderful letter penned by the Union hero to an old army comrade. Sheridan reveals that the famous black horse he rode during his frantic, morale-boosting race from Winchester to rally his routed troops at the Battle of Cedar Creek is still alive and well in his possession, noting: "He looks almost as well now as when you saw him in Virginia." Sheridan later renamed the black horse "Winchester." George H. Thomas on the Fitz John Porter Court-Martial (January 5, 1870): An autograph letter signed by the Union general known as "The Rock of Chickamauga." Thomas comments on the infamous Civil War court-martial of Gen. Fitz John Porter, who was relieved of command for alleged dereliction of duty during the Battle of Groveton. Thomas defends Porter's character, stating he never believed Porter willfully neglected his duty. George Washington Free Frank (Undated): A prominent, large ink signature reading "Go: Washington," scrawled as a free-franked address panel to a Connecticut cobbler named Joseph Webb. Historical records indicate Washington wrote to Webb primarily to check on custom orders for "horse skin" boots. George Washington on Long Island Plundering (October 31, 1778): A superb Revolutionary War-date letter signed by the Commander-in-Chief from his headquarters in Fredericksburg. Washington issues a stern reprimand to a local major after learning that Continental scouts traveling to Long Island under the pretext of gathering intelligence were indiscriminately plundering and distressing the local inhabitants. Washington commands him to stop the pernicious practice, explicitly ordering him to only employ those as spies or observers in whom he can place proper confidence. Daniel Boone Fayette County Survey (May 15, 1785): A mind-bogglingly rare complete manuscript document written and signed by the legendary pioneer as a Deputy Surveyor in Fayette County, Kentucky. Boone hand-writes the boundary logs for a 1,000-acre land plot using uncorrected frontier misspellings, tracing lines from "2 Shuger trees" to a "white oke and hickory." Boone tragically lost almost all of his own land in this exact county three years later due to title disputes. Simon Kenton Frontier Warrant (Undated): A financial document signed by the famous trans-Allegheny frontiersman who famously saved Daniel Boone's life during an Indian raid at Boonesborough. Science, Discovery, & Literature Benjamin Franklin (April 9, 1773): A magnificent 2-page autograph letter signed and initialed from London to "Dear Jenky" (Jane Parker). Franklin musters his immense powers of diplomacy to resolve a delicate financial disagreement with the family of his deceased New York printing business partner. To preserve their long family tie, Franklin delivers a timeless piece of advice: "But I think it contributes to the Duration of Friendship to keep its Accounts, & those of Business distinct & separate; and that an exact Justice in Pounds Shillings & Pence should be observed between Friends as between Strangers." Albert Einstein "World State" Manuscript (Undated, Post-WWI): A monumental 3-page unsigned autograph manuscript written in green ink. Einstein maps out a bold political plan for a unified "World State", arguing that the League of Nations failed because member states refused to surrender their individual sovereignty. He argues that a global political system is unconditionally necessary to stop our planet from becoming unbearable for humans, while warning that intellectuals often fail in politics because they lack quick decision-making and human people skills. Tantalizingly, the top of the page features a series of Einstein's handwritten mathematical equations in electromagnetics. Albert Einstein Signed Portrait (1935): A classic black-and-white portrait of Einstein in a tuxedo, beautifully inscribed in German to friends in remembrance of "happy musical evenings" spent playing his beloved violin. John Flamsteed (June 29, 1695): A rare signed financial receipt from the historic first Astronomer Royal of England. Flamsteed's meticulous star mapping directly provided the data Sir Isaac Newton used to verify his legendary theory of gravity. Raymond Chandler (November 5, 1946): A typed letter to his famous Hollywood agent, H.N. Swanson. Written right as Chandler abandoned the stress of the movie studios for the quiet coast of La Jolla, he tracks short story publishing rights while jokingly describing himself as "a guy who never says one thing when four will do." Samuel Francis Smith (December 4, 1893): A wonderful letter from the composer of "My Country, 'Tis of Thee", hoping his anthem kindles a spirit of freedom worldwide. Smith shares a lively reflection on aging, quoting Oliver Wendell Holmes Sr.'s birthday tribute to fellow hymn-writer Julia Ward Howe, noting that the human spirit can burn in perpetual youth if kept active. Herman Melville Defending Mardi (June 5, 1849): A magnificent 3-page autograph letter signed to his British publisher Richard Bentley (who would publish Moby-Dick two years later). Melville defends his new novel Mardi, which British critics had violently panned as too abstract and metaphysical, writing a timeless defense of the artist's mind: "But some of us scribblers, my Dear Sir, always have a certain something unmanageable in us, that bids us do this or that, and be done it must – hit or miss." He then reveals he is shifting ground away from the South Seas to write a plain, straightforward, amusing sea narrative with no metaphysics—his semi-autobiographical masterpiece, Redburn: His First Voyage. Melville letters are of legendary rarity. Claude Monet London Illness (March 14, 1901): A poignant 5-page letter handwritten in French on Savoy Hotel stationery to his wife. Monet gripes about a sudden illness that struck him down in London just as he was attempting one last creative effort to capture the Gothic spires of Westminster rising through the changing Thames fog, producing his legendary London Series of impressionist masterpieces. Franklin D. Roosevelt Founding the March of Dimes (April 7, 1927): A historic handwritten letter signed on legal stationery regarding the incorporation of the Georgia Warm Springs Foundation (later known nationwide as the March of Dimes). Paralyzed by polio, FDR details establishing the foundation as a non-profit rehabilitation center to help fellow polio victims find strength, creating one of his most enduring humanitarian health legacies. Jack London on The Call of the Wild (August 28, 1903): A mind-bogglingly rare autograph letter written in pencil to an early reader immediately following the publication of his masterpiece. London explains his creative structure for the novel, revealing his logic behind naming his legendary canine protagonist: "The only reason I named him Buck was that years before I had filed away among my notes as appropriate dog names ‘Buck’ & ‘Bright.’ ... I chose Buck – I guess because it was stronger than Bright." He beautifully adds: "We know little or nothing about what dogs think. But then we may conclude from their actions what their mental processes might be..." West Africa Slave Trade Uprising (January 15, 1808): A terrifying historical letter written by two slave traders aboard the Ship Hibernia near the St. Paul's River in Sierra Leone. Writing at the absolute peak of the Atlantic slave trade, they describe a massive, violent slave uprising where hundreds of local fighters descended upon their factory staging fort, plundering the stores, cutting the trader's hand, and forcing them to flee under cover of night. Letters detailing slave trade mutinies written directly from Africa are of immense historical scarcity. Hollywood, Sports, & Pop Culture Dwight D. Eisenhower (November 22, 1944): A deeply moving wartime letter written from Versailles to his wife, Mamie. The Supreme Allied Commander handles regular family business—enclosing $25 to help buy a durable Christmas gift for their son—before offering a somber look at the front lines: "Well sweet I’d like to think that this mess would be over soon... But the fighting and the dying go on – and the end is not yet. ‘Civilization’ is not pretty, when it resorts to war." Josephine Earp (March 3, 1929): An incredibly rare autograph letter signed by the wife of legendary gunfighter Wyatt Earp. Written just months after Wyatt's death, the former actress coordinates travel details while defending her late husband's untamed frontier legacy. Thomas Edison on Theodore Roosevelt (April 1919): An original autograph note scrawled on a poem written by a 13-year-old girl honoring the late President. Edison writes in pencil: "Some Girl! It’s in the blood capacity for high mental action accompanies the germ plasm..." 1951 Brooklyn Dodgers Signed Baseball: An official ball signed by 22 legendary members of the team, including Chuck Dressen, Gil Hodges, Pee Wee Reese, and Jackie Robinson. This historic ball dates to the exact, infamous season that culminated in Ralph Branca giving up the pennant-winning "Shot Heard 'Round the World" home run to the rival Giants. Ty Cobb Batting Advice Letter (September 14, 1954): A massive 5-page strategy letter written in green ink by "The Georgia Peach" to Pirates manager Fred Haney. Cobb offers dense, un-asked-for advice to pull a struggling hitter out of a slump, detailing exact hand placements, swinging parallels, and a warning to stop swinging for the fences. Cooperstown Hall of Fame Signed Bat: An official souvenir baseball bat signed boldly on the barrel by 13 legendary titans, including Ted Williams, Mickey Mantle, Willie Mays, Hank Aaron, and a highly controversial addition by Pete Rose. Irving Berlin Signed Sheet Music (1938): Vintage sheet music for "Alexander's Ragtime Band", beautifully inscribed by Berlin to fellow Academy Award-nominated Hollywood film composer Lew Pollack. Lucille Ball (Undated): A gorgeous sepia publicity photograph featuring her resting elegantly on a ship's helm, signed with warm sentiments. Josephine Baker (1935): A spectacular, oversized vintage photograph of the exotic stage dancer captured mid-performance, signed with a bold French inscription. P.T. Barnum (November 30, 1887): A beautiful letter written to a young boy, where the legendary showman lovingly promises that his traveling circus, "The Greatest Show on Earth", will be even larger, funnier, and more marvelous next year. George Gershwin An American in Paris Photograph (March 1929): An extraordinary sepia portrait showing the legendary composer seated at his piano. In the lower margin, Gershwin beautifully pens an autograph musical quotation consisting of four bars of music, mapping out the famous primary orchestral theme of An American in Paris just three months after its Carnegie Hall debut. Ira Gershwin MGM Movie Contract (December 27, 1949): A historic 6-page studio contract signed by the legendary lyricist for the Academy Award-winning MGM musical An American in Paris. The contract maps out his $56,250 pay structure and includes the famous studio "morals and conduct" clause used to keep contract players under the studio's thumb. John F. Kennedy & Robert Frost Inaugural Booklet (April 1961): A unique presentation copy of the limited-edition booklet printed for Robert Frost’s White House reception. It features Frost's dedication poem alongside the full text of JFK's historic "Ask not what your country can do for you" speech. It is signed by Kennedy on the cover and features a warm inscription from Frost to a journalist friend detailing the plane flight they shared. Ernest Hemingway Overseas Background Check (Undated): A jovial letter handwritten entirely in pencil to his hunting buddy Charles Thompson—the direct inspiration for "Karl" in The Green Hills of Africa. Hemingway requests that Thompson serve as a character witness for a government background check so he can travel overseas, writing with his signature wit: "If they interrogate you you can tell them what a good patriot, swell guy, always pay my debts (within two years or 20)..."Jerome Kern Signed Sheet Music (May 19, 1938): Vintage sheet music for the song "You Couldn't Be Cuter", inscribed to fellow film composer Lew Pollack. It is accompanied by a funny typed letter where Kern jokes that the song will probably be a "mummy by Decoration Day". Alex Haley Roots Inscription (June 25, 1984): A signed card featuring a good-natured sentiment referencing his ground-breaking saga, sending brotherly love from "Chicken George" and the family of Kunta Kinte. California Gold Rush Prospector Letter (July 25, 1849): A fascinating 3-page letter written by early 49er Mason R. Packer from Stockton, California, to his wife back east. Packer notes the exorbitant prices of basic goods in the boomtowns and coordinates his departure for the gold diggings near Sutter's Fort. The Honeymooners Cast Signed Photograph: A vintage publicity still showing the four core cast members (Jackie Gleason, Audrey Meadows, Art Carney, and Joyce Randolph) hanging out of a New York City bus window, signed beautifully by each actor. Charles Lindbergh Aviation Matte Portrait (Undated): A striking, oversized sepia waist-up portrait captured by Underwood & Underwood, showing Lindbergh standing proudly with the Spirit of St. Louis in the background, signed cleanly on the photographer's matte. Charles Lindbergh Leather Flight Portrait (Undated): A magnificent head-and-shoulders sepia portrait showing the youthful aviator clad in his complete leather flight jacket, helmet, and goggles, signed in bold black ink. Both Lindbergh portraits originated directly from the estate of the nation's very first federal aviation regulator, William P. MacCracken. The Little Rascals Vintage Signatures (1938–1939): A rare and highly desirable collector's set of five individual autograph leaves signed by the core childhood stars of the fabled Hal Roach Our Gang comedies, including Spanky McFarland, Buckwheat, Alfalfa, Darla Hood, and Porky Lee. Willie Mosconi Signed Billiard Ball Set: A complete presentation box containing fifteen individual billiard balls and an accompanying cue ball, each signed in full by the perennial 15-time world champion. The catalog notes his historic 1954 exhibition record where he sank an unbelievable 526 consecutive pool balls without a single miss. George S. Patton Cadet Letters (c. Fall 1903): A beautiful early letter written as a young cadet attending the Virginia Military Institute (VMI) to his aunt. Exhibiting his lifelong obsession with historical military tactics, the future general explicitly asks her to bring him white writing paper (rejecting blue paper as un-military) along with a newly published textbook entitled Strategy as Illustrated in British Campaigns. Richard Nixon Anti-Communist Speech (c. April 1953): A massive 15-page original typed speech layout containing extensive handwritten corrections and segregation notes by Vice President Richard Nixon. Plunging into a aggressive defense of his controversial role hunting down hidden Communists on the House Un-American Activities Committee (HUAC), Nixon defends the Alger Hiss investigations and prophetically maps out future international relations in East Asia. Roy Rogers & Gabby Hayes Signed Photo: A vintage 8x10 black-and-white publicity still showing both iconic Western screen stars in full costume, signed boldly across the image. Albert Schweitzer Aspen Visit (July 7, 1949): A striking portrait photograph of the philosopher and medical missionary, signed and dated during his historic summer visit to Aspen, Colorado. Piotr Ilyich Tchaikovsky Signed Cabinet Photo: An exceptional sepia vignette portrait photograph signed boldly across the image in Cyrillic script. The catalog hails this piece as perhaps the finest signed visual artifact of the legendary romantic composer in existence. Harriet Beecher Stowe Signed Quote: A crisp ink signature by the abolitionist author of Uncle Tom's Cabin, penning a biblical quote: "Trust in the Lord and do good." Booker T. Washington Tuskegee Appeal (January 27, 1894): A letter written on official school stationery to a New York judge. The iconic educator appeals for financial tuition sponsorships for poor but worthy Black students, written just one year prior to his historic "Atlanta Compromise" race-relations address. Mark Twain Faded Portrait (April 1909): A beautiful sepia-tone portrait showing the elderly humorist seated in a wooden chair, affectionately signed and inscribed: "Truly yours, Mark Twain. For Elizabeth."Elizabeth Taylor Nibbles and Me Hardcover (1946): A rare copy of the children's book written and illustrated entirely by a 13-year-old Elizabeth Taylor immediately following her breakout success in National Velvet. The book is warmly inscribed on the inside cover: "Lots of Love – From Nibbles & Elizabeth." Global Conflict & World War II Relics Erwin Rommel "Desert Fox" Postcard (September 9, 1939): A historic, mint-condition postcard handwritten in German by Rommel to his wife, Lucia Mollin, just eight days after the Nazi invasion of Poland sparked World War II. Rommel marvels at his new assignment commanding Hitler's guard battalion, writing with chilling confidence: "Things are going amazingly well for me... If we manage to maintain this pace, the war will be over in the West by the end of October, in my opinion." Admiral Chester Nimitz Propaganda handbill (February 1945): A wartime typed letter signed by Fleet Admiral Nimitz to an 1.1-year-old girl who shared his birthday. As a gift, Nimitz encloses an authentic U.S. propaganda bill dropped by Allied bombers over the Japanese mainland. The item is a 10-yen note printed on the back with a Japanese warning blasting the military cartel for wasting 5,000 yen per person on a losing war. Captured Okinawa "Rising Sun" Flag: An original silk Japanese military banner captured during the brutal Battle of Okinawa by a U.S. Army Major. The flag features printed margins translating to fierce nationalist slogans: "Our Military Strength Will Last Forever" and "Hoping for a Quick War." Gregory "Pappy" Boyington Flying Tigers Jacket: The authentic, black satin reversible flight jacket acquired directly from the estate of the legendary Marine Corps flying ace. The breast features embroidered stylized birds, the back showcases a fierce yellow tiger, and the reverse side maps out a detailed quilted green chart labeling major Japanese target cities around Mount Fuji. Charlie Owens D-Day Mapping Board (April 7, 1944): An original large perspective drawing accomplished in ink and pastel by the Los Angeles Times sketch artist. Dated exactly two months prior to the Allied invasion, the journalistic map utilizes sweeping arrows to project the exact troop movement paths that would be used on D-Day. Chaim Weizmann Palestine University Letter (July 10, 1903): A typed letter signed by the future first President of Israel, mapping out early zionist circulars to advocate for the foundation of a Jewish university in Palestine to combat academic discrimination in Europe.

metadata.description: Voyage du Sieur Paul Lucas au Levant, by Paul Lucas (Paris, 1704).  The download contains both volumes of this two-volume set, in 846 searchable and bookmarked pdf pages.  A Wikipedia entry (" Paul Lucas (traveller) ") describes the life and travels of this French merchant, naturalist, physician and antiquarian to Louis XIV.  He was in Egypt, the Levant, Armenia, Mesopotamia, Persia, and Asia Minor in the early 1700s. Religious communities were one of his interests, and he described the temples of ancient Egypt, and synagogues, churches, and mosques wherever he travelled.  Volume 1 mostly is devoted to Egypt: Alexandria, Cairo, the pyramids, Upper Egypt; Cyprus, Tripoli, Mt. Lebanon, Damascus, and northern Syria. Chapter 24 describes parts of Asia Minor, including Armenia,  Ararat, Erzerum, and the Kurds.  Volume 2 (chapters 1-3) continues the description of Armenia with a visit to Etchmiadzin, Erivan, Mt. Ararat, a narration of the legend of Saint Gregory and information on Armenian history.  Beginning with chapter 4 are descriptions of Tabriz, Media, Mesopotamia, Qom, Ispahan, Baghdad, Babylon, Nineveh, and Constantinople. Lucas encountered and described European missionaries such as the Jesuits and Capuchins, Armenian patriarchs, clerics, and merchants, and Muslim religious leaders. A recurrent observation concerns the avarice he experienced everywhere and from almost everyone--from secular rulers to religious leaders, from diplomats to the public at large.  Books digitized by Google and compiled by Robert Bedrosian.

Ronald Reagan kept building his case against Muam- mar Kaddafi-and hinting that the United States was ready to hit him again. This time the casus belli was the La Belle discotheque bombing in West Berlin. The president's counselor said they had worked up an "indisputable" trail of evidence connecting Libyan agents to the murderous blast. Two U.S. aircraft carriers took up positions within striking distance of Libya. Reagan suggested he was only waiting for clear battle conditions and a complete dossier on the Berlin case before striking. Turning up the rhetorical heat, he called Kaddafi "this mad dog of the Middle East." Going the boss one better, a senior U.S. official said, "We all know what you do with a mad dog." With the USS Coral Sea and the USS America both in the Mediterranean, one plausible scenario was that Reagan would send Navy jets from the carriers to bomb airfields. missile batteries, radar towers or other military targets along the Libyan coast. In addition. NEWSWEEK has learned, Washington has quietly asked Egypt to al- low the USS Enterprise. now stationed in the Indian Ocean. to pass through the Suez Canal to the Mediterranean. The presi- dent's advisers were confident they had the hardware to carry out a successful strike- and to best anything Kaddafi might throw back page 22i. United Nations Ambassa- dor Vernon Walters also left on a trip to London. feeding speculation that Washing- ton might try to launch a raid with U.S. Air Force FB-111 bombers based in Britain. The president's advisers were leaning against two other options: trying to take out Libya's oilfields or hitting suspected terrorist training camps. But there was still an outside chance they might go after some of those targets. As the days dragged on, however, it be- came increasingly difficult to sort out the administration's real intentions from mis- guided leaks and deliberate disinforma- IiQn? eagan's advisers were still dickering about what to do. Some members of the team argued they had been too slow and too public about preparing their attack. They advised waiting until Kaddafi's next out- rage, which they predicted could come any time. Washington had some good reasons for taking its time: it wanted to clinch the La Belle case, muster allied support and assemble maximum firepower. Making a virtue of necessity, some officials also ar- gued that the delay wore down the Libyans and kept them off balance. Still. the dawdling added to the risks in taking another poke at Libya. The unseem- ly dribble of leaked battle plans gave Kad- dafi plenty of time to get ready. One danger was that the Libyans would down or cap- ture American servicemen. "If I were a Navy pilot expecting to fly missions over Libya. I would be feeling very cross right now," said one Western diplomat in Wash- ington. "First they leak my targets. Now they delay things to give Kaddafi good time to prepare." Another peril was that Kaddafi might retaliate by launching terrorist attacks in the United States. But Americans are al- ready at risk. NEWSWEEK has obtained a summary of intelligence reports prepared v S. o cials that suggest that Kaddafi as stepped up surveillance of American citizens, businesses and government posts. According to the reports. U. . embassies in Greece and nearby NATO countries-prob- ably Italy and Turkey-are targets of Lib- van plots, as are U. S. embassies in 10 Afri- can countries. Three Libyan agents entered an African country with plans to attack the U.S. chancery and kidnap the ambassador. One U.S. ambassador in the Middle East has been targeted for assassination. In a Latin American country, a car with Libyan diplomatic plates was caught tailing a school bus filled with American children. Western sources have also uncovered evi- dence that Kaddafi is offering to pad Iran and Islamic Holy War in Lebanon S100 million for the six Americans they are hold- ing. An intelligence has learned that Kaddafi is plotting to attack U.S. "commer- cial interests"-primarily banks-in Eu- rope and the Middle East. Long struggle: In any event, Washington faced the risk of a protracted. escalating struggle, and some of Reagan's advisers worried that Americans may not have the stomach for that kind of fight. Over the long run. strategists believed that the Eu- ropean allies and the moderate Arabs would support a move to get tougher with Kaddafi-and that the Soviets didn't care enough about their mercurial ally to allow his fight with Washington to upset arms- control talks or planning for another sum- mit. Even so. another round with the colo- nel-particularly if it got bloody-could fray U.S. relations with all of those parties. Although the dangers were clear, the president's aides argued strongly that they had ample cause for taking a second crack at Kaddafi. After the Gulf of Sidra skir- mishes, they had hoped to deter Libya's terrorist a ventures ea in what U.S. inte tgence new about them to the pres ( EWSWEEK, April 7. But as one top U.S. official put it, Kaddafi's suspected role in the West Berlin bombing and several other attacks since then suggest that "he's decid- ed to go ahead no matter what." Privately, the president and his senior aides conceded that their test of wills with Kaddafi might not end until Kaddafi was dead. They had no intention of trying to do the job them- selves. but they hoped America's military pressure might encourage disgruntled Lib- yan officers to move against their leader. There were reports Reagan might decide against a strike if the allies agreed to tough- er economic and political measures against Libya. Otherwise, his aides said. the presi- dent could still give the "go" order. 'Proportional response': The debate turned on the policy of"proportional reponse" that Reagan approved at a National Security Council meeting on March 14. The doctrine. which holds that the force of U.S. retali- ation should match the strength of Kad- dafi's attacks, was the brainchild of national-security adviser Vice Adm. John Poindexter t page 24 i. and it played a crucial role in persuading reluctant Defense De- partment officials to agree to challenge the Libyans in the Gulf of Sidra. This time. senior U.S. officials said. the Joint Chiefs of Staff laid out a full range of military options for Reagan and the National Security Coun- cil immediately after the Berlin bombing. Over the next three days new reconnais- sance photos were reviewed and the list of targets was narrowed; then Reagan ap- proved an attack "in principle." Defense Department officials were ready to move quickly. At the Pentagon, NATO commander Gen. Bernard Rogers and chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff Adm. William Crowe reviewed the firepower Declassified in Part - Sanitized Copy Approved for Release 2011/12/19: CIA-RDP9O-00965ROO0707060060-9 Declassified in Part - Sanitized Copy Approved needed to carry out a strike. Pentagon offi- cials were determined to stick to the criteri- on of "proportionality"-and they read that as meaning an attack on limited targets such as the radar array around Tripoli. Then, according to Defense De- partment officials, the president and his other advisers decided to consider larger targets such as Libya's airfields. The mili- tary brass went back to the drawing board. During most of the week the president had the guidance of advisers whc were bull- ish on retaliation: Poindexter, Shultz and White House chief of staff Donald Regan. Two officials who favored greater restraint were out of town: Defense Secretary Caspar Weinberger was in Asia and Australia, and Vice President George Bush was in the Persian Gulf. Over the weekend they both returned to Washington. and the president was expected to consult them before mak- ing a final decision. Through most of the deliberations Reagan kept his options open, according to a senior official. But he did insist on several preconditions for a strike: that Kaddafi's link to the Berlin bombing be firmly established; that any raid pose minimum risk to civilians, and that an attack entail an "acceptable ratio" of potential U.S. casualties. Of all the options. the most likely to meet Reagan's guidelines was sending jets from the carriers to hit Libyan military posi- tions. Most of those targets lie along the northern coast, reducing the exposure of Americans to hostile fire or capture. Ad- ministration officials were eager to ground the Libyan Air Force, which has bases at Umm Aitiqah, Okba ibn Nafa and Al Adem. either by destroying runways or at- tacking parked planes' If Kaddafi's ships sailed out to take on the Sixth Fleet, com- manded by Vice Adm. Frank Kelso. there was the possibility of attacking naval bases at Benghazi and Tripoli. During the Gulf of Sidra confrontation. U.S. bombers took out a radar tower at a SAM-5 missile battery in Sirte. But the Libyans quickly rebuilt it, apparently with the help of Soviet advisers and free-lance British engineers. U.S. in- telligence indicated they were also scram- bling to complete a SAM-5 position in Ben- ghazi. If the United States went after the missile sites again, administration sources said, it would hit the radar antennas, then follow up by destroying the launchers and any missiles stored nearby. The administration had also not ruled out a longer range hit. From the start the Pentagon had liked the option of dispatch- ing the British-based FB-llls, which can move fast, fly low and carry a heavy bomb- load. At first, according to British officials. Prime Minister Margaret Thatcher was cool toward the proposal. But the sources said she warmed up after U.S. officials let the British see their full file on Kaddafi's links to the La Belle blast. As Vernon Wal- ters left for Europe, Thatcher was said still not to like the idea of using Britain as a staging area but to be willing to go along if Reagan insisted. In another sign the ad- ministration might be leaning toward the Britain scenario, several U.S. tanker air- craft, which could be used for in-flight refu- eling, took wing for American air bases in the United Kingdom. The president's advisers rejected other possibilities as too dangerous. The CIA had identified some three dozen camps where it suspected the Libyans of training terror- ists. But top U.S. officials argued that strikes on those targets might also hit civil- ians. Senior planners pointed out that an attack on Libyan oilfields, pumping sta- tions and loading docks could endanger in- nocent oil workers, including Americans and Europeans. Senior officials said they gave only limited consideration to a joint ground operation with Egypt-a move that Arab diplomats in Washington advised could have disastrous consequences for Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak. Intercepted messages: While it weighed its military choices, the administration also worked to tie Kaddafi to the Berlin bomb- ing. Senior officials in Washington echoed reports that U.S. intelligence had inter- cepted messages between Tripoli and the Libyan People's Bureau in East Berlin. In late March, they said, Tripoli instructed the bureau to carry out an undisclosed " lan." On April 4 the bureau informed its capital that the operation would take place soon. Hours later-after the attack on the discotheque-the Libyans in East Berlin reported that they had executed the plan. Then on April 6 Tripoli exhorted other People's Bureaus to follow East Berlin's example. The Washington sources also sec- onded what NATO commander Rogers said after a speech in Atlanta: that U.S. com- manders had gotten wind of an imminent attack and tried to alert nightspots favored by American servicemen-but that they were "15 minutes too late" to save La Belle. White House officials were eager to man- age the evidence, however, both because they wanted to make sure it was accurate and because they wanted to wait for an offi- cial announcement until they were ready to take military action. As a result, they re- fused to back up two top-level officials who went public prematurely. One was Rogers, who went on the record after his address in Atlanta. The other was U.S. Ambassador to West Germany Richard Burt, who bragged about the administration's goods on the "Today" show. According to one Reagan aide, White House officials didn't dispute the information Burt mentioned, but they were "looking for more." They also charged Burt with being publicity hungry. ""Some people can't avoid kissing a television cam- era when it's pointed at them." sniped one senior Reagan official. When the president did lay out his case against Kaddafi, he was likely to cite more than the La Belle blast. Senior U.S. officials said they had intelligence about Libyan involvement in a rocket attack against the American Embassy in Beirut last week and in two other terrorist plots since the Gulf of idra showdown. They said one was a plan to assassinate U.S. Ambassador to France Joe Rodgers; however, both French and Western sources in Paris denied knowl- edge of such a plot. C.S. intelligence sources said Kaddafi recently instructed two Lebanese Army officers with close ties to Syria to ""activate" a plan to kill A meri- can -diplomats in Beirut. The sources also said a number of detecting Libvanagents- including some Libyans. but mostly Pales- tinians. North Africans and Vest urope- ans_had rovided details on Libyalots against Americans. But only the British were shown raw transcripts of the intercepted Libyan messages. The oth- er allies saw paraphrases. That appeared to explain why the West Germans sounded circumspect about the evidence in the La Belle case, even though they verified the thrust of Washington's allegations, Re- sponding to U.S. pressure. the French threw out two Libyan diplomats two weeks ago. Last week Bonn also expelled a couple of Libyan envoys. But the allies continued to resist U.S. requests to shut down the People's Bureaus or to impose tougher eco- nomic sanctions against Kaddafi. Since pri- vate U.S. firms still do a lot of business with Libya, they maintained that Washington"s demands were hypocritical. In addition. they repeated their longstanding argu- ment that sanctions don't work. Many Europeans also worried that Rea- gan's war with Kaddafi had become coun- terproductive-and they were joined in that concern by many Arab diplomats and U.S. foreign-policy analysts. The skeptics argued that bloodying Kaddafi might only make him more of' a hero to his people. "Kaddafi would have to hire every" Madi- son Avenue PR firm to get what Reagan is providing him with." said one French offi- cial. They also stressed that even if Libya's troublemaking was stopped. terrorists would still get aid and comfort from the likes of Syria, Iran and the Soviet Union. "Terrorism has been around forever and it is going to be with us forever." pointed out Gary Sick. a former NSC officer under Jim- my Carter. As Reagan and Kaddafi moved closer to the next round in their grudge match, however, those calculations ap- peared almost moot. The world's most techno- logically formidable arsenal is squaring off against an Arab power with far more bluster than brawn. The biggest chal- lenge is defeating Libya's air defenses-and inflicting enough damage to keep Kad- dafi's forces from rebuilding as they have done before. Blinding enemy air defenses is the first priority in a surgical strike. U.S. fighters, bombers and electronic-warfare planes streaking off the carrier decks would work much like a foot- ball offense with some players clearing a path for the player carrying the ball. Navy A-6E Intruders and A-7E Corsair bombers are the deadly ball carriers. Sophisticated F/A-18 Hornet and F-14A Tomcat fighters would take on any Libyan jets sent up to inter- cept the air armada. EA-6B Prowler aircraft would provide vital support by fooling ene- my radar. Each Prowler car- ries five long pods under its wings to listen for enemy radar signals; on-board computers match them against a stored "library." pinpointing their source. Specialists on board distort the radar pulses, send- ing back false readings about the aircraft's altitude and course. A Libyan radar opera- tor might think he saw many planes, or his screen might be snowed like a broken TV set. Wire spaghetti: The standard attack plan is to run two U.S. strike groups toward the en- emy radar at once. One group would consist only of EA-6B's, trying to look like as many air- craft as possible; the other would consist of attack planes, trying to look inconspicuous. To determine which was the attack force, Libyan oper- ators would have to leave their radar transmitting- long enough, theoretically, for U.S. bombers to close in, launch their missiles and peel for home. Their HARM's (high- speed anti-radiation missiles) would zero in on the ra- dar beams at speeds up to Mach 2, their 46-pound war- heads shredding the transmit- ting grids into wire spaghetti. Also in HARM's way: radio towers near Tripoli that serve vital communication roles. With its radar blinded, Lib- ya's Soviet-made SAM anti- aircraft missiles would be vir- tually useless. Other U.S. attack planes could follow in and destroy the SAM's with Rockeye cluster bombs. The Rockeyes-each releasing 247 armor-piercing darts-could also make Swiss cheese out of any Libyan planes sitting on Kaddafi's airstrips. To destroy aircraft in hangars, the Navy has CBU-72 explosive bombs that spray 200 pounds of fuel in a fine aerosol, then ignite the cloud, creating a wave of pressure strong enough to col- lapse almost any structure. More firepower, Fully destroy- ing Libyan airfields or oil fa- cilities would require more firepower than carrier-based aircraft provide. But Air Force B-52s flying from stateside bases or FB-111s from U.S. bases in Britain could pulver- ize either. Both could be refu- eled in midair by KC-135 tank- ers, hit their targets and return home without stop- ping. Kaddafi's new SAM-5s are designed to thwart such high-flying B-52s, so destruc- tion of the missiles by low- flying carrier-based planes would be an essential prelude. Kaddafi's defenses have oth- er weaknesses. SAM radars are difficult to operate in hot climates; they overheat at midday and freeze at night. And they are only as good as their operators; Libya has few trained technicians. The lack of skilled pilots is also the Achilles' heel of Libya's Air Force, already outclassed by the Navy's Tomcats, Hornets and their high-tech air-to-air missiles. Facing those odds, six Syrian pilots on loan to Libya refused to take off in Kaddafi's Soviet-made MiG's during last month's Gulf of Sidra dustup, and Libya mounted little air challenge. Kaddafi's missile ships, meanwhile, would run up against the Navy's Har- poon antiship cruise missiles. Launched from A-6E Intrud- ers or cruisers like the York- town, the huge sea-skimming Harpoons have built-in radar to home in on moving targets. There are plenty of oppor- tunities for problems. Two car- rier-based planes were shot down over Lebanon in 1983, and Libyan air defenses are more formidable than those. Last month U.S. HARM mis- siles managed to knock out only one of seven radars at Lib- ya's SAM-5 site near Sirte, and even one operating SAM-5 could do serious damage. But on paper at least, Kaddafi's forces are heavily outnum- bered, which is exactly what U.S. strategists hope he knows. ,MELINDA BECK 111th JOHN BARRY In Washin'ton Declassified in Part - Sanitized Copy Approved for Release 2011/12/19: CIA-RDP90-00965R000707060060-9 Declassified in Part - Sanitized Copy Approved for Release 2011/12/19: CIA-RDP90-00965R000707060060-9 In HARM's Way: Soviet-built SAM-2 antiaircraft missiles Targets of Opportunity MisuratT- j 0110- Na j A Missile bases defenses Radar rcasist S.
